screens.title: Iteration: Refining Your Game Design
screens.subtitle: A practical path from quick prototypes to polished gameplay

narration.text: In this lesson we focus on iteration, the steady, repeatable process that turns a raw game idea into a playable, polished experience. Iteration is not a single event but a cycle: build a quick prototype, test it with players, analyze what you observe and hear, and then apply focused changes. Over time those small changes compound into meaningful improvements. You will learn how to collect useful playtest feedback, detect true patterns in player data, prioritize what to change, and apply incremental fixes that don’t break other systems. We’ll also cover essential tools and habits — like version control — that make experimentation safe and reversible. You’ll see a concrete example: adjusting a jump mechanic in a platformer by changing a couple of variables, re-testing, and measuring the result. Finally, we’ll discuss decision moments: when to keep iterating, when to pivot the design, and when a prototype has reached a stage you can call an MVP or vertical slice. By the end of this chapter you’ll have a practical workflow for refining game systems and a checklist for turning player reactions into targeted improvements.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Iteration is a repeating loop: prototype, playtest, analyze feedback, and implement small, focused changes to refine gameplay while preserving your core vision.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll build in this chapter

narration.text: In this chapter you will develop a set of practical skills for refining game systems through iteration. First, you will learn the full iterative loop: prototype, playtest, analyze, and iterate. That sequence is the scaffold you'll use to make measurable improvements. Second, you will practice techniques for interpreting playtest feedback. We'll focus on finding patterns, separating signal from noise, and categorizing issues by severity and frequency so your fixes address root causes. Third, you will learn how to implement changes incrementally and why small, isolated changes let you test their effect without introducing new regressions. Fourth, you will get an introduction to version control as a safety net: branching to test ideas, and reverting when an iteration creates problems. Each objective includes a concrete milestone you can verify with a simple playtest or repository check. By the end of these exercises you'll have both a mental checklist and practical steps for turning player observations into targeted improvements, and you'll be able to demonstrate those skills on a small prototype.

screens.title: What is Iterative Design?
screens.subtitle: A working definition and why it beats one-shot design

narration.text: Iterative design is a continuous cycle of building a quick prototype, testing it with players, analyzing the results, and applying focused improvements. That loop repeats until the game reaches the intended quality or the team decides on a different direction. The important claim is that iteration treats design as discovery rather than a single correct blueprint. A prototype surfaces assumptions quickly: you learn whether a mechanic is fun, confusing, or broken by exposing it to real play. Concrete example: a prototype platformer jump may reveal that players miss timing windows or can't read jump arcs. That observation becomes the basis for a testable change, like tweaking jump force or adding visual cues. A common misconception is that iteration means endless tinkering; in practice, iteration is disciplined. You make small, reversible changes, evaluate their effect, and document results. This prevents churn and lets you isolate what worked. The takeaway is that iteration reduces risk by converting opinions into data and gives you a safe path to improve the game incrementally. Ask yourself after each round: what measurable change did this iteration produce?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Iteration is discovery-focused: small experiments, rapid tests, and measured adjustments rather than large one-time redesigns.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › What is Iterative Design?
Definition
Iterative Design

A repeating cycle of prototype, playtest, analyze, and iterate used to discover what actually works in a game.

Analogy
Think of iteration as sculpting with feedback. Each pass removes rough edges revealed by players.
Common mistake
Treating every suggestion as mandatory instead of spotting patterns and aligning fixes with your vision.
Concrete example
Prototype observation: Players report the jump feels "floaty" and timing is inconsistent. Hypothesis: increase gravity and add variable jump height to give tighter control. Iteration: tweak gravity multipliers and add low-jump behavior. Re-test to confirm improved responsiveness.
Key takeaway
Small experiments give measurable signals; they guide the next iteration.
Check your understanding
Can you state one measurable metric you would use to validate a jump change?
Why this fills the canvas: definition, example, misconception, and takeaway are grouped for clear learning.

screens.title: The Iterative Loop
screens.subtitle: Prototype → Playtest → Analyze → Iterate, step by step

narration.text: The iterative loop has four clear steps and each serves a different role. Prototype: create a quick, playable slice that tests one or two core assumptions. Keep assets and polish minimal so you can iterate faster. Playtest: watch players interact without explaining everything; observe behavior and note both actions and language they use. Record frequency of issues and any confusion points. Analyze: look for patterns across sessions. Group feedback by frequency and severity, and convert observations into testable hypotheses. Prioritize issues that break or obscure the core experience. Iterate: implement a small change that directly addresses a hypothesis, and keep it isolated so you can measure its effect. Example: if multiple players fail the same jump, test whether adjusting jumpForce or adding visual cues solves the problem. A common misconception is to change many things between tests; this obscures which adjustment fixed the problem. Instead, make one or two targeted changes, then run another short playtest. The core insight is testability: every iteration should produce an observable outcome that informs the next round. The Iterative Loop means each iteration must produce a testable hypothesis and one measurable change so you can identify what improved the player experience.. In practical terms, prototype → playtest → analyze → iterate, step by step. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Stepwise loop
keyIdea.text: Each iteration must produce a testable hypothesis and one measurable change so you can identify what improved the player experience.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › The Iterative Loop
Prototype
Build a minimal playable slice that isolates the assumption you want to test. Keep time and assets low.
Playtest
Observe players, take notes, and log how often issues happen. Prefer in-person observation or recorded sessions when possible.
Analyze
Group feedback by frequency and severity. Turn observations into specific hypotheses: "Players miss the jump because jump arc is too high."
Iterate
Implement one or two focused changes, then re-test to measure impact. Document the outcome before the next round.
Example workflow
Observation: 6 of 8 players fail the same platform jump. Hypothesis: lower jump arc or add midpoint platform. Change: reduce jumpForce by 10% and add visual cue. Re-test with 6 players and compare success rate.
Misconception
Avoid making many simultaneous changes; you won’t know which change affected player behavior.
Pro tip
Label each build and keep a short changelog so results are traceable across iterations.
Key takeaway: each loop must yield an observable result you can compare to the previous build.

narration.text: Analyzing feedback is both a scientific and a design judgment exercise. The goal is to find recurring problems and to understand their severity and root cause. Start by collecting raw notes, recording sessions, and simple metrics like success rate or time to complete a task. Then categorize comments: frequency (how many players saw this), severity (does it block progression or is it cosmetic), and alignment with your core vision. A concrete example: if three players mention the same obstacle is unclear, and it prevents progress, that is high frequency and high severity — a top priority. If one player suggests a new feature that conflicts with your vision, treat it as low priority unless many players independently express it. Common misconception: treating every vocal suggestion as equally important. Instead, prioritize patterns and the issues that cause failure or frustration. Use simple tools — a spreadsheet or card board — to map feedback to priority and assign an owner. The final step is to create a hypothesis for the highest priority item and design a focused test for the next playtest.

keyIdea.title: Analysis rule
keyIdea.text: Prioritize fixes that are both frequent and severe; document the reasoning and create a testable hypothesis for each prioritized item.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Analyzing Playtest Feedback
Collect
  • Record sessions and take time-stamped notes.
  • Log simple metrics: success rates, time-to-complete, error counts.
  • Include direct player quotes for clarity.
Categorize
Group feedback by frequency and severity. Tag items that block progression as high priority.
Prioritization matrix
High frequency / High severity: Fix first
High frequency / Low severity: Triage
Low frequency / High severity: Investigate context
Low frequency / Low severity: Consider later
Concrete example
If many players miss a platform jump, mark it high frequency and high severity and form a hypothesis to test a specific change like reducing jump arc.
Pro tip: track items in a simple sheet or Trello board and include a column for hypothesis and test results.

screens.title: Prioritization Strategies
screens.subtitle: Severity, Frequency, and Alignment with Vision

narration.text: Prioritization is the act of deciding which issues to fix first. There are three lenses you should combine: severity, frequency, and alignment with your game's core vision. Severity answers whether the issue blocks progression or harms a core mechanic. Frequency measures how many players experience the issue. Alignment checks whether the suggested change moves the game toward the experience you intend. For example, if players find an enemy unfair and it prevents progression for many players, it’s high severity and high frequency and should be prioritized. If a single tester suggests a new mechanic that doesn't match the game's vision, deprioritize it despite the test's enthusiasm. A common pitfall is chasing feature requests that please vocal testers but harm the intended experience for the target audience. Practical strategy: create a two-axis card board or spreadsheet, mark severity and frequency, and add a short note about vision alignment. Assign a priority and one person responsible. After the next playtest, record whether the fix improved the measured metric. That loop of prioritize, change, and measure is how iteration becomes disciplined and productive.

keyIdea.title: Prioritization rule
keyIdea.text: Prioritize items that are both frequent and severe and that align with your core design goals; de-emphasize one-off suggestions that conflict with vision.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Prioritization Strategies
Severity
Does this issue prevent players from progressing or substantially reduce enjoyment?
Frequency
How many players encountered the problem? Use counts or percentages from your sessions.
Vision alignment
Will the suggested change move the game toward the experience you intend for your target players?
Practical tool
Use a simple table with columns: Issue, Frequency, Severity, VisionMatch (Yes/No), Priority, Assigned. Add a hypothesis and a target metric for each prioritized item.
Example
Problem: Jump is floaty. Frequency: 75% of testers. Severity: Blocks level completion. Vision match: Yes. Priority: High.
Pitfall
Over-optimizing for a single tester who is not representative of your target audience.
Takeaway: combine the three lenses to create defensible, testable priorities for iteration.

screens.title: Implementing Incremental Changes
screens.subtitle: Make focused edits, test, and measure effects

narration.text: When you implement changes from playtest analysis, do so incrementally and deliberately. An incremental change is a small, well-defined edit to one variable, mechanic, or level geometry that you can isolate and test. This discipline prevents regressions and makes cause-and-effect clear. A concrete example from the chapter: to address a floaty jump, you might adjust two variables: moveSpeed and jumpForce, or add a fall multiplier to increase gravity while falling. Make a single change or at most a couple of related changes, run a short playtest, and compare measured outcomes such as jump success rate or subjective ratings of responsiveness. Avoid overhauls between tests; changing many things at once makes it impossible to know what worked. Another practical habit is to add brief annotations to your version control commit messages like "jump: reduce jumpForce 10% — hypothesis: reduce floatiness" and tag builds used in playtests. This creates a traceable history so you can revert if a change introduces new problems. The key is observable improvement: after each incremental edit, you should be able to say whether the metric improved and by how much.

keyIdea.title: Incremental rule
keyIdea.text: Change one focused parameter or design element at a time, test, and measure so you can attribute improvements to specific edits.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Implementing Incremental Changes
Step-by-step
  1. Identify a single hypothesis derived from playtests.
  2. Make one focused change (variable, geometry, feedback).
  3. Label the build and commit with a clear message.
  4. Run a short, targeted playtest and collect the same metrics.
  5. Compare results and decide next action.
Example changes
Adjust jumpForce, add fallMultiplier to increase gravity when falling, or add platform geometry to reduce gap size. Each change should be tested alone when possible.
Documentation
Keep a short changelog: build label, change summary, hypothesis, test date, and measured outcome. This prevents repeated experimentation blind to past results.
Key takeaway
Small, labeled changes make iteration traceable and reversible.
Common mistake
Overhauling multiple mechanics between tests prevents clear attribution and slows learning.

screens.title: Modifying Player Movement — Practical Code Example
screens.subtitle: A safe, testable tweak to jump and fall behavior

narration.text: This screen walks through a practical code change you might perform during iteration. The goal is to make the jump feel snappier by adding a fall multiplier and variable jump height. The code snippet shows public variables for moveSpeed, jumpForce, fallMultiplier, and lowJumpMultiplier so you can tweak them in the editor. The logic checks for grounded state and applies an impulse for a jump. During ascent, if the player releases the jump button early, a low-jump multiplier applies extra gravity to shorten the jump. During descent, a fall multiplier increases gravity so the character falls faster and feels less floaty. Concrete example: changing fallMultiplier from 1 to 2.5 often makes landings feel more responsive. A misconception to avoid is editing many physics parameters at once; change one value, run a short playtest, and compare the result. After the change, label the build and re-run the same playtest tasks to measure success rate and subjective responsiveness. Modifying Player Movement — Practical Code Example means expose tuning variables and make small, commented commits so each code change maps to a single hypothesis and test.. In practical terms, a safe, testable tweak to jump and fall behavior. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Code insight
keyIdea.text: Expose tuning variables and make small, commented commits so each code change maps to a single hypothesis and test.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Modifying Player Movement — Practical Code Example
Starter code (read-only)
// PlayerMovement.cs (excerpt)
public float moveSpeed = 7f; // Adjusted for snappier feel
public float jumpForce = 12f;
public float fallMultiplier = 2.5f; // Makes falling faster
public float lowJumpMultiplier = 2f; // For variable jump height

private Rigidbody rb;
private bool isGrounded;

void Start()
{
  rb = GetComponent();
}

void Update()
{
  // Movement omitted for brevity
  isGrounded = Physics.Raycast(transform.position, Vector3.down, 1.1f);
  if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
  {
    rb.AddForce(Vector3.up * jumpForce, ForceMode.Impulse);
  }

  if (rb.velocity.y < 0)
  {
    rb.velocity += Vector3.up * Physics.gravity.y * (fallMultiplier - 1) * Time.deltaTime;
  }
  else if (rb.velocity.y > 0 && !Input.GetButton("Jump"))
  {
    rb.velocity += Vector3.up * Physics.gravity.y * (lowJumpMultiplier - 1) * Time.deltaTime;
  }
}
Teaching notes
  • Expose tuning variables as public fields so designers can iterate without code changes.
  • Adjust one variable at a time and record the build label and hypothesis.
  • Use FixedUpdate for physics changes and keep input handling separate for clarity.
Example test: change fallMultiplier from 1.5 to 2.5, run 6 playtests, measure jump landing consistency, and collect subjective feedback on "snappiness."
Remember: the code is a tool for controlled experiments. Commit with a message that states the hypothesis for future traceability.

screens.title: Activity: Iterating on Jump Mechanics
screens.subtitle: A guided lab to practice the loop in your Unity prototype

narration.text: This activity walks you through a focused iteration on jump mechanics in a Unity prototype. Begin by forming a clear hypothesis from playtests: for example, "Players report the jump is floaty, so adding a fall multiplier will reduce floatiness." Open your PlayerMovement script, expose moveSpeed, jumpForce, fallMultiplier, and lowJumpMultiplier as public fields, and implement the extra gravity logic for falling and variable jump height. Make one small change — say, increase fallMultiplier to 2.5 — and commit the change with a short message describing the hypothesis. Then schedule a quick playtest with 4–6 players using the same tasks as before. Collect both objective metrics (did players complete the jump?) and subjective feedback (do they feel more responsive?). Analyze the results: did success rates improve? Did any new problems appear? If the change helped, you can keep it or make a smaller follow-up tweak. If it didn’t, revert the change using version control and try an alternative, such as reducing gap width or adding a visual cue. The discipline of forming hypotheses, making small edits, and measuring outcomes is the heart of productive iteration.

keyIdea.title: Activity goal
keyIdea.text: Practice a full iteration on a single mechanic: form hypothesis, change one variable, test, and record outcomes to learn which edits actually improve the experience.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Activity: Iterating on Jump Mechanics
Steps
  1. Form a hypothesis from playtest notes.
  2. Make one small change in PlayerMovement.cs and commit with a hypothesis message.
  3. Run 4–6 short playtests and collect same metrics as before.
  4. Compare outcomes and decide next action: keep, tweak, revert, or try another hypothesis.
Starter checklist
Label the build, record metrics, capture recordings or notes, and assign one owner to drive the next iteration.
Example observation
Observation: Players overshoot platforms. Hypothesis: increase gravity when falling. Change: set fallMultiplier to 2.5. Test: run 6 players through the same jump task and measure success rate.
Reflection prompt
After testing, ask: did objective metrics improve and did players report better control? If not, what next hypothesis will you try?
Safety tip
Use version control to create a branch for each experiment so you can compare and revert safely.

screens.title: Version Control for Iteration
screens.subtitle: Why Git (or similar) is indispensable for experiments

narration.text: Version control records the history of your project so experiments are safe and reversible. When iterating, use branches to try different solutions concurrently — for example, create a branch for "jump-ease" and another for "jump-visuals." Each branch can implement a distinct hypothesis and be playtested independently. If a change introduces regressions, you can revert to the main branch without losing work. For solo developers, version control prevents accidental loss and provides a timeline of decisions, which is particularly helpful when you later revisit a mechanic. A common error is making big changes on the main branch without labeling or commits that explain the hypothesis. Instead, craft clear commit messages like "jump: increase fallMultiplier to 2.5 — hypothesis: reduce floatiness; test with 6 players." This practice makes it possible to trace which change produced which outcome. After successful experiments, merge selective commits into the main branch. If experiments fail, close the branch and keep the learning. Version control turns iteration from a messy trial-and-error process into a controlled experimentation platform. Version Control for Iteration means use branches to experiment, clear commit messages to document hypotheses, and merges to adopt successful changes while keeping history intact.. In practical terms, why git (or similar) is indispensable for experiments. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Version control rule
keyIdea.text: Use branches to experiment, clear commit messages to document hypotheses, and merges to adopt successful changes while keeping history intact.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Version Control for Iteration
Why it matters
Version control lets you experiment safely, revert bad changes, and compare branches used for different hypotheses during playtests.
Workflow
  1. Create a branch for the experiment.
  2. Make the focused change and add a hypothesis to the commit message.
  3. Test on the branch, record outcomes, and merge if successful.
Concrete example
Branches: main, jump-ease, jump-visuals. Each branch contains specific edits. Playtest independently and keep the branch that meets your metric thresholds.
Common mistake
Making experimental commits without clear messages or build labels. That makes it hard to know which experiment produced a change in player behavior.
Pro tip: use semantic commit messages that include the hypothesis and the playtest date for quick traceability.

screens.title: When to Pivot vs. When to Iterate
screens.subtitle: Recognize signs that a design needs a fundamental change

narration.text: Knowing when to keep iterating and when to pivot is one of the hardest design judgments. Iteration is the first response: try focused fixes, gather more data, and document outcomes. Pivot when repeated, well-designed iterations fail to address core issues, or when feedback reveals that the fundamental concept does not meet the needs of the target audience. For instance, if many iterations on a combat mechanic still produce the same player frustration and the mechanic conflicts with your desired pacing, a pivot in approach may be necessary. A pivot can be subtle — adjusting the role of a system — or dramatic, like changing core mechanics or genre. Before pivoting, make sure you've exhausted reasonable iterations that isolate root causes. Keep in mind the cost of pivoting and the project's timeline: sometimes freezing features and moving to polish or an MVP is the correct path instead of deeper iteration. The key is to use structured experiments and clear acceptance criteria so the decision to pivot is based on evidence, not fatigue or opinion. When to Pivot vs. When to Iterate means pivot only after structured iterations fail to resolve core problems and evidence suggests the current approach is not viable for the intended audience.. In practical terms, recognize signs that a design needs a fundamental change. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decision rule
keyIdea.text: Pivot only after structured iterations fail to resolve core problems and evidence suggests the current approach is not viable for the intended audience.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › When to Pivot vs. When to Iterate
Signs to iterate more
  • You can form clear hypotheses that still haven’t been tested.
  • Incremental edits produce partial improvement.
  • Changes are low cost and quick to test.
Signs to consider a pivot
  • Repeated iterations don’t resolve the core problem.
  • Feedback consistently points to a misfit with the target audience.
  • The cost of further iteration outweighs potential gains.
Practical checklist before pivoting
Confirm you ran controlled experiments, documented outcomes, tried multiple hypotheses, and evaluated timeline and resource costs. If the evidence favors a pivot, plan one clearly and keep the lessons learned from previous iterations.

screens.title: Playtest Design and Practical Tips
screens.subtitle: How to run useful playtests and collect reliable data

narration.text: Designing and running playtests well is essential to productive iteration. Start with a clear goal: what hypothesis are you testing and what metrics will indicate success? Keep sessions short and focused, using the same set of tasks for each player so results are comparable. During the test, observe silently and take time-stamped notes; video or screen recordings help you review behavior later. Ask a few targeted post-test questions to gather subjective impressions but avoid leading questions. Practical example: when testing a jump, ask players to attempt a sequence of three jumps of increasing difficulty and note success, retries, and comments. Record objective metrics like success rate and time-to-complete and subjective ratings like perceived responsiveness. Use simple tools — a spreadsheet, Trello board, or a short form — to capture frequency and severity of issues. A common mistake is changing the test conditions between sessions, which invalidates comparisons. Keep tasks consistent and only change the build between iteration rounds. The result will be reliable data that can guide prioritization and hypothesis selection for your next iteration. Playtest Design and Practical Tips means run short, consistent sessions with clear tasks and measurable outcomes so comparisons across builds are meaningful and actionable.. In practical terms, how to run useful playtests and collect reliable data. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Playtest rule
keyIdea.text: Run short, consistent sessions with clear tasks and measurable outcomes so comparisons across builds are meaningful and actionable.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Playtest Design and Practical Tips
Before the test
  • Define the hypothesis and the metric you will track.
  • Create consistent tasks for each player.
  • Label builds and commit messages for traceability.
During the test
  • Observe silently and take time-stamped notes.
  • Record objective and subjective measurements.
  • Keep environments and tasks consistent across players.
After the test
Analyze patterns, prioritize by frequency and severity, create testable changes, and document outcomes. Use the same tasks in the next round so you can make fair comparisons.

screens.title: Common Iteration Mistakes and Pro Tips
screens.subtitle: Avoid these traps and establish helpful habits

narration.text: There are recurring mistakes teams make during iteration. First, changing too many variables between tests. This makes it impossible to attribute improvements. Second, treating every suggestion as mandatory: not all player ideas align with your vision. Third, skipping version control or failing to label builds, which causes lost work and confusion. Fourth, over-iterating without defined acceptance criteria; you can spend cycles improving low-impact items. To avoid these, adopt a few habits: make one change per test when possible, write commit messages that record the hypothesis, keep a changelog, and set simple acceptance criteria for each prioritized issue. Pro tips: keep prototypes lightweight, lean into short tests with consistent tasks, and use small sample sizes early to detect big problems quickly. Another tip is to prioritize fixes that reduce player friction rather than those that add new features. A closing question to guide your practice: after an iteration, what single metric will you check to decide if a change succeeded? Common Iteration Mistakes and Pro Tips means don’t overhaul many systems at once; document hypotheses; use version control; and focus on high-impact fixes aligned with your vision.. In practical terms, avoid these traps and establish helpful habits. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid these

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.4 › Common Iteration Mistakes and Pro Tips
Top mistakes
  • Making many changes between tests.
  • Treating one-off suggestions as priorities.
  • Not using version control or clear commit messages.
  • Iterating without acceptance criteria.
Pro tips
  • Change one thing and test it.
  • Label builds and include hypothesis in commit messages.
  • Prefer lightweight tests that reveal major problems fast.
  • Focus first on reducing friction before adding complexity.
Reflection prompt
After your next iteration, identify one metric that will confirm whether a change truly improved the experience. Use that metric to decide keep, tweak, or revert.

Version Control

Record changes, use branches for experiments, and revert or merge based on results.

Incremental Changes

Make small edits so their effects are measurable and reversible.

Pivot

If structured iterations repeatedly fail, consider a change in direction based on evidence and cost analysis.

Iteration is a disciplined practice: hypotheses, measured changes, versioned experiments, and evidence-based decisions lead to better game design.
